own_scenes.desc: En Gran Bretaña el LSD circulaba por el mismo tipo de gente que en Estados Unidos: estudiantes de arte, hipsters, bohemios y poetas, muchos llegados desde la CND. Su primera gran reunión fue la International Poetry Incarnation del Albert Hall (junio de 1965: Ginsberg, Trocchi, Burroughs, Adrian Mitchell), filmada por Peter Whitehead. En enero de 1966 John Hopkins y Steve Stollman montaron en el Marquee el primer Spontaneous Underground, intento, como los Acid Tests, de crear un entorno que se acercara a la disrupción perceptiva del LSD; el 13 de marzo, «The Trip», con el grupo de improvisación AMM y el debut en el Marquee de unos Pink Floyd que dejaban las versiones de R&B. En febrero Barry Miles y John Dunbar abrieron la librería Indica (ESP-Disk, Burroughs, Leary, Artaud, Crowley, Gurdjieff, Blavatsky), con la ayuda de Paul McCartney. En abril Miles y Hopkins repartieron en la marcha de la CND THE Global moon-edition Long Hair TIMES.

notes.text: La London Free School de Notting Hill, con la trabajadora social Rhuane Laslett y Michael X, quería unir a una comunidad pobre y diversa: de su Fayre de septiembre, con la steel band de Russ Henderson, nació el carnaval de Notting Hill. Para recaudar fondos tocaron en el salón de All Saints los Pink Floyd, recién fichados por Peter Jenner y Andrew King, que habían grabado a AMM (Extracts from a Continuous Performance, improvisación sin ensayos ni discusión). Syd Barrett, tras su primer LSD, escribió casi todas sus canciones en 1966 («Interstellar Overdrive», nacida de una versión tarareada del «My Little Red Book» de Love; «Matilda Mother», «The Gnome»), entre el cosmos, Lewis Carroll y los traumas de la guerra. El 15 de octubre la All-Night Rave del Roundhouse, con Soft Machine, Yoko Ono y McCartney, lanzó International Times: «el cambio empieza por ti».

refs.q: The first major gathering of this subculture was the June 1965 International Poetry Incarnation at the Albert Hall
refs.para: The first major gathering of this subculture was the June 1965 International Poetry Incarnation at the Albert Hall, where an audience of several thousand witnessed performances by Allen Ginsberg, Alex Trocchi, William Burroughs, Christopher Logue, Gregory Corso and many others. Harry Fainlight prevailed through several hecklers to finish his mescaline nightmare ‘The Spider’, while Adrian Mitchell brought the house down with ‘To Whom It May Concern’, with its refrain, ‘Tell me lies about Vietnam’.
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: During February, Miles opened up Indica in partnership with the art dealer John Dunbar
refs.para: During February, Miles opened up Indica in partnership with the art dealer John Dunbar, right next to the Scotch of St James club in Mason’s Yard. The idea was to pull together the various strands of experimental art and literature in one place, to reflect the new consciousness. The shop stocked a selection of records (ESP-Disk material and the spoken-word album Call Me Burroughs), the latest poetry magazines and a wide selection of books – from Nietzsche, Burroughs, Timothy Leary and beyond to Antonin Artaud, Aleister Crowley, George Gurdjieff and Madame Blavatsky – a treasure trove of arcana.

refs.q: It would feature the avant-garde improv group AMM, along with the Marquee debut of a young group called the Pink Floyd
refs.para: On 13 March, Stollman advertised the latest Spontaneous Underground event as ‘The Trip’. It would feature the avant-garde improv group AMM, along with the Marquee debut of a young group called the Pink Floyd, who were morphing from R&B covers into something less formalised. The girlie magazine Titbits covered the event: ‘What a rave! A man crawling naked through jelly. Girls stripped to the waist. Off-beat poetry. Weird music. It all adds up to Raving London. For the capital no longer swings. It goes berserk!’
refs.chapter: Abril: The Third Eye: el LSD y sus descontentos

refs.q: The featured group was the Pink Floyd, and this was their first show with their new management team
refs.para: The featured group was the Pink Floyd, and this was their first show with their new management team, Andrew King and Peter Jenner. The group had played several of Steve Stollman’s Spontaneous Underground events at the Marquee and, on 12 June 1966, Jenner saw them and decided to get involved. ‘Through the Fugs, which were avant-garde, and the Stollman connection, they put on the thing where I saw the Floyd. It was a Happening at the Marquee. So I thought, “That’s great. We had the label, we need some avant-garde pop music.”’

refs.q: This was the coming-out ball of the underground, held to launch the International Times
refs.para: This was the coming-out ball of the underground, held to launch the International Times, a new magazine hot off the press. The idea that had begun in the spring with THE Global moon-edition Long Hair TIMES had finally come to fruition in a biweekly tabloid that aimed to crystallise the London underground. Barry Miles and John Hopkins were involved, but it was edited by Tom McGrath, who was not sympathetic to the West Coast scene and ‘resisted any whole-hearted move in that direction’.
